challengeCorner.prompt: A store has goods available at cost $42,000, at retail $70,000. Net sales were $63,000. Compute the cost ratio and the estimated ending inventory at cost.

discoveryHook.scenario: A clothing store knows its cost of goods available and the retail selling prices. By calculating a [[kw:cost ratio]] (cost ÷ retail), it can estimate the cost of ending inventory from the retail value of unsold goods. This is the [[kw:retail method]], often used for interim financial statements.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: The cost ratio is not a fixed number; it should be recalculated each period. [[imp:Changes in markups or markdowns affect the ratio.]]

questions.prompt: Cost ratio = Goods available at cost ÷ Goods available at ___.

visuals.title: Retail Method Example
visuals.caption: Cost ratio links retail value to cost value.

formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Cost Ratio} = \frac{\text{Goods Available at Cost}}{\text{Goods Available at Retail}}$$ $$\text{Ending Inventory at Retail} = \text{Goods Available at Retail} - \text{Net Sales}$$ $$\text{Ending Inventory at Cost} = \text{Ending Inventory at Retail} \times \text{Cost Ratio}$$
formulaCard.title: Retail Method Formulas
notes: Net sales = Gross sales – Returns and allowances.
The cost ratio should reflect the relationship between cost and retail for the current period.

explanation: The [[kw:retail method]] estimates ending inventory cost by converting retail prices to cost using a cost‑to‑retail ratio.
Steps: 1. Calculate goods available at cost and at retail. 2. Compute the cost ratio: $$\text{Cost Ratio} = \frac{\text{Goods Available at Cost}}{\text{Goods Available at Retail}}$$.
3. Subtract net sales (at retail) from goods available at retail to get ending inventory at retail. 4. Multiply ending inventory at retail by the cost ratio to estimate ending inventory at cost.
[[imp:This method is useful for interim reports and insurance claims, but still requires a physical count for annual statements.]]

blocks.title: 2. Gross Profit Method of Estimating Inventory

visuals.caption: The method relies on a stable gross profit rate.
visuals.title: Gross Profit Method Example

notes: GP rate = Gross Profit ÷ Net Sales (historical).
If GP rate is given as a percent of cost, adjust accordingly.
formulaCard.title: Gross Profit Method
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Estimated COGS} = \text{Net Sales} \times (1 - \text{GP Rate})$$ $$\text{Ending Inventory} = \text{Goods Available at Cost} - \text{Estimated COGS}$$

explanation: The [[kw:gross profit method]] estimates ending inventory based on the historical relationship between gross profit and net sales.
Steps: 1. Calculate the gross profit rate: $$\text{GP Rate} = \frac{\text{Gross Profit}}{\text{Net Sales}}$$.
2. Estimate COGS = Net sales × (1 – GP rate).
3. Ending inventory = Goods available at cost – Estimated COGS.
This method is often used after a disaster or when physical counts are not possible.
[[imp:It assumes the gross profit rate is stable; changes in pricing or theft can distort the estimate.]]

teacherCues: Explain that this method uses the historical gross profit rate to estimate COGS and then ending inventory.

discoveryHook.scenario: A fire destroys a store's inventory. To file an insurance claim, the owner must estimate the lost inventory cost. Using the [[kw:gross profit method]], if sales were $100,000 and the store normally has a 40% gross profit rate, estimated COGS = $100,000 × (1 – 0.40) = $60,000. Then ending inventory = Goods available – $60,000.

steps: Days to sell = 365 ÷ 6 ≈ 60.8 days.

teacherCues: Define inventory turnover: how many times inventory is sold and replaced in a period.
Formula: Inventory Turnover = COGS ÷ Average Inventory.

visuals.title: Inventory Turnover Calculation
visuals.caption: The store turned over its inventory 5 times during the year.

explanation: [[kw:Inventory turnover]] measures how many times a company's inventory is sold and replaced over a period (usually a year).
Formula: $$\text{Inventory Turnover} = \frac{\text{Cost of Goods Sold}}{\text{Average Inventory}}$$.
Average inventory = (Beginning inventory + Ending inventory) ÷ 2.
A higher ratio indicates faster sales and less money tied up in inventory.
[[imp:Turnover varies widely by industry; compare with industry benchmarks.]]

formulaCard.title: Overhead Allocation

explanation: [[kw:Overhead]] (indirect costs) includes expenses like rent, utilities, insurance, and management salaries that benefit multiple departments.
Since these cannot be directly traced, they are allocated using a reasonable basis.
Common allocation bases: [[kw:floor space]] (square footage), [[kw:sales volume]], number of employees.
Allocation formula: $$\text{Department's Share} = \text{Total Overhead} \times \frac{\text{Department's Base}}{\text{Total Base}}$$.
[[imp:The choice of allocation base should reflect the cause‑and‑effect relationship with the cost.]]

steps: Total area = 1,000 sq ft.

blocks.title: 5. Blueprint Aid for Inventory Estimation and Overhead Allocation

formulaCard.title: Inventory Estimation & Overhead Blueprint
notes: Retail method: cost ratio = cost/retail; ending inventory = ending retail × ratio.
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{COGS (GP method)} = \text{Sales} \times (1 - \text{GP rate})$$ $$\text{Ending Inventory} = \text{Goods Available} - \text{COGS}$$ $$\text{Allocated Overhead} = \text{Total Overhead} \times \frac{\text{Dept Base}}{\text{Total Base}}$$

visuals.title: Blueprint: Gross Profit Method & Overhead Allocation
visuals.caption: Separate sections for each type of problem within the blueprint.

rows.1: GP rate 30%, net sales $150,000, goods available $130,000. Also, rent $6,000, dept X 200 sq ft, Y 400 sq ft.

explanation: Apply the blueprint to hybrid inventory/overhead problems:
1. Understand: identify which method is required (retail, gross profit, turnover, or overhead), and list the given data.
2. Solve: apply the appropriate formulas step‑by‑step. For inventory estimation, compute COGS and ending inventory. For overhead, compute allocation fractions and dollars.
3. Conclude: verify that estimates are reasonable (e.g., ending inventory cannot be negative), and that allocated overhead sums to the total.
This ensures you don't confuse the methods or ignore key data.
